segments.name: The Child of the Rue Saint-Honore

stops.name: Eglise Saint-Roch, Paris: baptized on the day of his birth
stops.date_confidence: attested. fr.wikipedia gives the birth on the rue Saint-Honore and the baptism the same day at Saint-Roch; MacTutor and en.wikipedia agree on the date. The pin is the church of Saint-Roch, not the birth house, whose number is not recorded in any source reached.
stops.campa: A son is born on the rue Saint-Honore five weeks after the Bastille falls, and is carried the same day up the street to Saint-Roch for baptism. His father, Louis-Francois Cauchy, is a lieutenant de police of the order that is at that moment being taken apart around him. The child is named Augustin-Louis. The street outside is the one along which the tumbrils will pass, and the family will spend the next five years learning what the new order costs a policeman of the old one. Nothing in the parish entry marks the day as anything but ordinary.
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of Saint-Roch, rue Saint-Honore, for 21 August 1789
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Arcueil: the half pound of bread
stops.date_confidence: the move is attested, the year is not settled. MacTutor and en.wikipedia render it loosely as 'at age four', giving c. 1793; fr.wikipedia ties the retreat specifically to the aftermath of the execution of Thiroux de Crosne on 28 April 1794. Safest reading: c. 1793-94, during the Terror. The date here orders the segment and should not be quoted as a fact. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from charles_babbage.journey.json and erik_satie.journey.json, which both pin Arcueil at 48.7994, 2.3336; note that OSM puts the Arcueil town centre some 800 m north of that, a discrepancy inherited with the pin and flagged in the report rather than fixed here. The quotation is given by MacTutor as Cauchy's own letter from Arcueil, which would make him about five when he wrote it.
stops.campa: The Terror closes on Paris and Louis-Francois moves his household south to Arcueil, out of reach of the section committees and the bread queues. The boy is four, then five. Food in the village is rationed to almost nothing: half a pound of bread on a good day, hard crackers and an allotment of rice to stretch it. The scientists of Paris will make this village famous for something else entirely within fifteen years. For now it is a house held together by a policeman with no police left to command, and the boy learns his first letters there from his father.
stops.quote: We never have more than a half pound of bread - and sometimes not even that. This we supplement with the little supply of hard crackers and rice that we are allotted.
stops.quote_source: Cauchy, letter from Arcueil during the Terror, quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics, citing B. Belhoste, Augustin-Louis Cauchy: A Biography (1991)
suggested_refs: B. Belhoste, Augustin-Louis Cauchy: A Biography (1991), on the Arcueil years
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Ecole Centrale du Pantheon, Paris: Latin before mathematics
stops.date_confidence: the schooling in 1802-1804 and its classical content are attested by MacTutor and en.wikipedia; the month is not recorded and defaults to January. The story that Lagrange, a visitor at the family table, advised the father to keep the boy off mathematics until he had languages is biographical tradition running through Belhoste, unverified in this pass and marked as tradition in the prose. Lagrange has no atlas file; he is queued only.
stops.campa: Lagrange, the tradition says, is a visitor at the family table, and tells Louis-Francois not to let the boy near mathematics yet: languages first. The father obeys. At the Ecole Centrale du Pantheon the son reads Latin and Greek, writes verse in both, and takes prizes for it. He will build a proof the way he is taught here to build a period, in clauses that have to hold. Two years of grammar and prosody stand between him and the subject he will spend fifty years rebuilding. He turns to mathematics in 1804, at fifteen.
suggested_refs: The site of the Ecole Centrale du Pantheon, later the Lycee Henri-IV, Place du Pantheon
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Ecole Polytechnique, Paris: second of two hundred and ninety-three
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, the examiner and the placing. en.wikipedia: 'In 1805, he placed second of 293 applicants on this exam and was admitted'; MacTutor names Biot as examiner and Lacroix, de Prony, Hachette as teachers with Ampere as analysis tutor. Month not recorded. Coordinate corrected from the research pool's 48.8459, 2.3499 to the OSM value for the historic Montagne Sainte-Genevieve campus at 1 rue Descartes; the pool's value fell about 160 m south on rue Clovis and was reused at three separate entries.
stops.campa: Jean-Baptiste Biot examines him for entrance and he places second among some two hundred and ninety-three candidates. Inside he finds Lacroix, de Prony and Hachette teaching, and Andre-Marie Ampere set over him as tutor in analysis. He is sixteen, and in two years he will leave for the engineering school, having placed near the top of everything put in front of him. The school is Napoleon's: militarized, drilled, turning out artillery officers and state engineers, and the mathematics taught in it is the most advanced in Europe and is taught to boys in uniform.
suggested_refs: The Ecole Polytechnique buildings on the Montagne Sainte-Genevieve, 1 rue Descartes
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Ecole des Ponts et Chaussees, Paris: the canal and the state engineer
stops.date_confidence: the 1807-1810 attendance is attested by MacTutor and en.wikipedia, and en.wikipedia attests the Ourcq Canal work; Pierre-Simon Girard as the named supervisor comes through the dossier and is reconstruction. The completion 'with highest honors' is en.wikipedia's wording, reported rather than documented from an examination record, and is treated as reconstruction. Month not recorded.
stops.campa: He enters the state school of bridges and roads and is sent out as a trainee onto the Ourcq Canal, the works cutting water from the Marne country down into the basin at La Villette to supply Paris. The training is not theory. It is embankments, masonry, the pressure of water against a wall, the behaviour of a continuous body under load. The mathematics of continua he will still be writing forty years later begins in a trench. He finishes in 1810, at twenty-one, reportedly at the head of his year.
suggested_refs: The Canal de l'Ourcq and the Bassin de la Villette, Paris, the trainee works of 1807-1810
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Cherbourg: the arrival with Laplace in the luggage
stops.date_confidence: attested for the posting and for March 1810 as its start, by MacTutor and en.wikipedia. The four-book luggage list, Laplace, Lagrange, Virgil and the Imitation of Christ, comes through Belhoste as digested in the dossier; MacTutor independently carries the two mathematical volumes. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from louis_xvi.journey.json and georges_sorel.journey.json, which both pin Cherbourg at 49.6462, -1.6157.
stops.campa: He is posted aspirant-ingenieur to Cherbourg, where Napoleon is building the greatest artificial harbour in Europe against England. He arrives in March with four books in his luggage: Laplace's Mecanique celeste, Lagrange's Theorie des fonctions analytiques, Virgil, and the Imitation of Christ. He rises at four. He works the day on the port and the night on the two mathematical volumes, and writes home that the labour does not tire him but feeds him. He is twenty, and one of the junior engineers on a state project of the first rank.
stops.quote: I get up at four o'clock each morning and I am busy from then on. ... I do not get tired of working, on the contrary, it invigorates me and I am in perfect health...
stops.quote_source: Cauchy, letter home from Cherbourg, 1810, quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics, citing Belhoste (1991)
suggested_refs: The Digue de Cherbourg and the Rade de Cherbourg, begun under Louis XVI and continued by Napoleon
louis_xvi.journey.json, for the royal inspection of the same breakwater in June 1786
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Cherbourg: the charge of pride
stops.date_confidence: the letter is attested to 1810 by MacTutor, citing Belhoste; the month is not given and defaults here to October to sit after the arrival. Nothing in the record fixes the season.
stops.campa: The engineers of the port take his religion badly. He hears himself called proud, arrogant, self-infatuated, and writes to his mother that the charge is devotion misread, that he has done nothing but keep his own practice. The pattern is set at twenty and will hold for forty-seven years, through every chair he is refused and every seat he is given. Then, he tells her, the subject is dropped: nobody mentions religion to him any more, and he is left alone with it. He does not raise it with the engineers again.
stops.quote: So they are claiming that my devotion is causing me to become proud, arrogant and self-infatuated. ... I am now left alone about religion and nobody mentions it to me anymore...
stops.quote_source: Cauchy, letter to his mother, 1810, quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics, citing Belhoste (1991)
suggested_refs: The 1810 Cherbourg correspondence to Marie-Madeleine Cauchy, printed in Belhoste (1991)
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Cherbourg: the rigidity of the polyhedron
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1811 by MacTutor for the polyhedra theorem and to 1812 for the further papers on polygons and polyhedra, with Legendre and Malus named as the men encouraging him from Paris. Month not recorded.
stops.campa: Legendre and Malus write from Paris encouraging him to send work. He is doing mathematics in the hours the harbour leaves him, in a port town two hundred miles from any library that matters. What he sends is a theorem about solids: a convex polyhedron built of rigid faces hinged at the edges cannot flex, and the shape of the faces determines the angles between them. The thing is settled, immovable, provable in a few pages. It is the first mathematics of his that the Institute has to take seriously.
suggested_refs: Cauchy's rigidity theorem for convex polyhedra, 1811, and the 1812 papers on polygons and polyhedra
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Cherbourg: the return through illness
stops.date_confidence: September 1812 is attested for the departure by both MacTutor and en.wikipedia. The nature of the illness is not: modern historians debate whether it was physical illness or a depressive episode, and the surviving evidence does not permit a secure clinical judgement. The prose says so rather than choosing.
stops.campa: Two years of four o'clock risings end in collapse. In September he leaves the harbour works and goes back to Paris ill, and does not return to Cherbourg. He is twenty-three and has just lost the career the state trained him for. He keeps the salary, on leave, for three more years, and spends them on mathematics. What the illness was, the record does not say; later biographers have read depression into it and cannot prove it, and the contemporary word is simply that he is unwell and overworked.
suggested_refs: The engineering leave records of the Corps des Ponts et Chaussees, 1813-1815
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Institut de France, Paris: the memoir on symmetric functions
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1812 for the submission and 1815 for the publication in the Journal de l'Ecole Polytechnique, by MacTutor and en.wikipedia. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from evariste_galois.journey.json, itself inherited from joseph_fourier.journey.json, which pins the Palais de l'Institut on the quai Conti at 48.8566, 2.3376.
stops.campa: In November he lays before the Institute a memoir on symmetric functions and on the number of values a function can take when its variables are permuted. He is on sick leave from an engineering corps, unemployed in fact, reading his own work to the most powerful scientific body in Europe. It is a young man's paper, and at its centre is the beginning of a theory of substitutions that will pass down through Evariste Galois and the whole century after him. Publication waits until 1815.
suggested_refs: Memoire sur le nombre des valeurs qu'une fonction peut acquerir, Journal de l'Ecole Polytechnique (1815)
evariste_galois.journey.json, for the theory of substitutions carried forward
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Institut de France, Paris: fifty-three votes and none of them his
stops.date_confidence: the pattern of repeated failure to obtain an Institute seat in 1813-1815 is attested by MacTutor and en.wikipedia, with the Bureau des Longitudes place going to Legendre and the geometry seat to Poinsot. The specific count of zero votes out of fifty-three is reconstruction: it reaches the pool through Belhoste as digested in the dossier and was not checked against a primary register. The 1814 memoir on definite integrals is attested. Month not recorded.
stops.campa: He stands for a seat at the Institute and is beaten twice over: the Bureau des Longitudes place goes to Legendre, the geometry section to Poinsot. In the same stretch he publishes the memoir on definite integrals in which the ideas of his complex analysis are already lying in plain sight, waiting a decade for their author to recognise them. The body that will not have him is being handed, that year, the foundation of his reputation. In one ballot, by a count the biographies repeat without a register to back it, fifty-three votes are cast and none of them is his.
suggested_refs: Memoire sur les integrales definies (1814)
The proces-verbaux of the Academie des sciences for the 1814 elections, not consulted
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Ecole Polytechnique, Paris: assistant professor of analysis
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor and en.wikipedia: the mechanics chair went to Jacques Binet, Cauchy took the assistant professorship of analysis and the second-year course, and was promoted to full professor after an initial one-year contract. Month not recorded. Coordinate corrected as at the 1805 stop.
stops.campa: The chair of mechanics goes to Jacques Binet. What Cauchy gets instead is the assistant professorship of analysis and the second-year course, which is to say the whole of the calculus as it is taught to the future engineers of France. He begins by refusing to teach it the way it has been taught. Infinitesimals of unstated size, series summed without asking whether they converge, functions manipulated on faith: all of it goes. The lectures are harder than the students want, and the school's administrators complain about it for the next fifteen years.
suggested_refs: The second-year analysis course of the Ecole Polytechnique, 1815-1830
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Institut de France, Paris: the Grand Prix for the propagation of waves
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1816 by MacTutor and en.wikipedia. Month not recorded. The memoir's later importance, its Lagrangian formulation of the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations with three conserved invariants, is not stated in the campa because its rediscovery is a twentieth and twenty-first century matter; it is carried in the refs instead.
stops.campa: The Academie awards him its Grand Prix for a memoir on the propagation of waves on the surface of a heavy fluid, a problem set out of the mechanics of water and answered with the analysis he has been building since Cherbourg. The same body gave him nothing at all two years earlier, and is no longer able to overlook him. The prize is the first unambiguous public verdict in his favour after four years of being passed over. He is twenty-seven. The memoir runs to some three hundred pages.
suggested_refs: The 1815 prize memoir on wave propagation, and its Cauchy invariants
Uriel Frisch and Barbara Villone, arXiv:1402.4957 (2014), on the memoir's long disappearance and recovery
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Institut de France, Paris: the seat that Carnot and Monge vacate
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor and en.wikipedia for March 1816 and for the fact that the seat opened through the Bourbon Restoration purge that removed Lazare Carnot and Gaspard Monge. That contemporaries held the manner of entry against him is biographical tradition; the judgement that his mathematics already met Academy standard is the research pool's and is not a source's words.
stops.campa: The Restoration purges the Academy. Lazare Carnot, regicide, and Gaspard Monge, Bonaparte's man and founder of the Polytechnique, are struck from the rolls by royal ordinance, and the seats are filled by appointment rather than election. One of them is given to Cauchy. His mathematics is beyond question and the manner of his entry is not; the republicans of the section never forget how he came in. He takes his place among men who have just watched two of their own removed for politics, and he is a declared royalist and a declared Catholic.
suggested_refs: The royal ordinance of 1816 removing Carnot and Monge from the Academie des sciences
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: College de France, Paris: standing in for Biot
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1817 by MacTutor, which gives Biot's departure for the Shetland Islands as the occasion and names integration methods and convergence as the subject. Month not recorded.
stops.campa: Biot leaves Paris for the Shetland Islands to measure the shape of the earth, and Cauchy takes his lectures at the College de France. The Cours d'analyse is four years off and is already being spoken aloud, week by week, to whoever is in the hall. Between the Polytechnique course, the College substitution and the Academy, he now holds three of the four rooms in Paris where French mathematics is decided. He teaches integration and the convergence of series to an audience that did not sign up for rigour and gets it anyway.
suggested_refs: Biot's 1817 geodetic expedition to the Shetland Islands, which opened the College de France substitution
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Eglise Saint-Sulpice, Paris: the marriage to Aloise de Bure
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia: 'Aloise and Augustin were married on April 4, 1818, with great Roman Catholic ceremony, in the Church of Saint-Sulpice.' The daughters' birth years, 1819 and 1823, are attested by the same article. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from victor_hugo.journey.json, which pins Saint-Sulpice at 48.8514, 2.3342.
stops.campa: He marries Aloise de Bure at Saint-Sulpice with full Catholic ceremony. She is the daughter of Marie-Jacques de Bure, bookseller and printer to the trade, and the marriage puts the professor inside the house of his own publisher: De Bure freres will print the Lecons and much else that carries his name. He is twenty-eight, settled, salaried, at the exact centre of the mathematics of his country. Nothing in the arrangement suggests that in twelve years he will walk out of France alone and leave the three of them behind. Two daughters follow, Marie-Francoise Alicia in 1819 and Marie-Mathilde in 1823.
suggested_refs: The marriage register of Saint-Sulpice, 4 April 1818
The house of De Bure freres, booksellers and printers, rue Serpente

stops.name: Maison Trudon, Sceaux: the summers begin
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the start date: the c. 1822 summers at his wife's family property at Sceaux come through Belhoste as digested in the dossier, and are corroborated only indirectly by fr.wikipedia's account of his death 'dans la maison familiale de sa femme a Sceaux'. Month chosen to signal a summer residence, not recorded. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from eugene_grasset.journey.json and the other atlas Sceaux files, which pin the town at 48.7784, 2.2903.
stops.campa: From about this year the household summers at Sceaux, in a property of his wife's family south of Paris. The town is a few miles out and a world off: gardens, air, the noise of the Polytechnique left behind. He keeps the habit for thirty-five years. It is where he writes when Paris will not let him work, where he will pay for a girls' school and a boys' patronage out of his own pocket in old age, and where, in a bedroom on this property, he will die. He is thirty-three when the habit begins.
suggested_refs: The Maison Trudon at Sceaux, the de Bure family property
sources: B. Belhoste, Augustin-Louis Cauchy: A Biography (1991), via the working dossier

segments.name: The Rigor and the Referee's Table

stops.name: Institut de France, Paris: Poncelet on the pavement
stops.date_confidence: the Poncelet quotation is attested, given in full by MacTutor; the framing of the encounter as a harsh refereeing of the projective geometry after Cauchy's 1820 criticism comes through the dossier's summary of Belhoste and is reconstruction as to date and circumstance. Month not recorded. Poncelet has no atlas journey file and does not appear in QUEUE.md.
stops.campa: Jean-Victor Poncelet, who worked out projective geometry as a prisoner of war in Russia, submits it to the Academy and Cauchy reports on it harshly. Poncelet goes to his house to argue, catches him leaving, and gets a walk down the street instead of a hearing. Poncelet writes it down decades later, still exact about how short the walk was. In a few minutes, he says, he understood that he had earned neither regard nor respect, and was told to wait for the referee's own forthcoming Lecons, where the question would be very properly explored. Then the referee walked off.
stops.quote: ...I managed to approach my too rigid judge at his residence ... just as he was leaving ... During this very short and very rapid walk, I quickly perceived that I had in no way earned his regards or his respect as a scientist ... without allowing me to say anything else, he abruptly walked off, referring me to the forthcoming publication of his Lecons a l'Ecole Polytechnique where, according to him, 'the question would be very properly explored'.
stops.quote_source: Jean-Victor Poncelet, recollection of Cauchy's treatment of him after Cauchy's 1820 criticism of his work on projective geometry, quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics
suggested_refs: Poncelet, Traite des proprietes projectives des figures (1822), and the Academy report on it
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Ecole royale polytechnique, Paris: the Cours d'analyse
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1821 by MacTutor and en.wikipedia. Month not recorded. The reach of the book's consequences is the research pool's judgement rather than a source's wording, and is stated as a plain claim.
stops.campa: The Cours d'analyse de l'Ecole royale polytechnique is printed, written for second-year engineering students who did not ask for it. In it a limit is defined, a continuous function is defined, a convergent series is defined, and every one of the definitions is framed in terms that can be checked. What had been an art of manipulation producing results known to be right becomes a discipline in which the right to a result must be earned. Half the propositions of the eighteenth century do not survive contact with the book.
suggested_refs: Cours d'analyse de l'Ecole royale polytechnique (1821)
Bradley and Sandifer, Cauchy's Cours d'analyse: An Annotated Translation (Springer, 2009), the first full modern English version
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Ecole royale polytechnique, Paris: the Resume des lecons
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1823 by MacTutor and en.wikipedia for the Resume des lecons donnees a l'Ecole royale polytechnique sur le calcul infinitesimal, and by en.wikipedia for the birth of Marie-Mathilde in the same year. Month not recorded for either.
stops.campa: Two years later comes the Resume des lecons donnees a l'Ecole royale polytechnique sur le calcul infinitesimal, and with it the definite integral defined as a limit of sums rather than assumed as an inverse of the derivative, and the mean value theorem put to work as a tool rather than quoted as an observation. The students still complain. The administrators still ask him to teach something simpler and faster. He does not. His second daughter, Marie-Mathilde, is born the same year.
suggested_refs: Resume des lecons donnees a l'Ecole royale polytechnique sur le calcul infinitesimal (1823)
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Institut de France, Paris: the calculus of residues
stops.date_confidence: the formal development of the calculus of residues in 1826 is attested by en.wikipedia and MacTutor, and the integral theorem in full developed form is attested to 1825 by en.wikipedia. The start of the Exercices de mathematiques as a self-published annual serial in 1826 is reconstruction, resting on the standard Belhoste-derived account as digested in the dossier and not re-checked against a bibliographic record. Month not recorded.
stops.campa: He begins issuing the Exercices de mathematiques, a yearly serial he writes entirely himself and controls entirely himself, and in it he sets out the calculus of residues: at a point where a function of a complex variable breaks down, a single number is left behind, and the sum of those numbers around a closed path settles the integral. He calls the new object a residue, the part that remains. Definite integrals that had resisted every real method fall to it in a line.
stops.quote: Residues arise ... naturally in several branches of analysis ... . Their consideration provides simple and easy-to-use methods, which are applicable to a large number of diverse questions, and some new results ...
stops.quote_source: Augustin-Louis Cauchy, Sur un nouveau genre de calcul analogue au calcul infinitesimal (1826), English rendering as given on Wikiquote
suggested_refs: Sur un nouveau genre de calcul analogue au calcul infinitesimal (1826)
The Exercices de mathematiques, annual, 1826-1830
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Institut de France, Paris: Abel's memoir on the referees' table
stops.date_confidence: the 1826 submission of Abel's memoir on transcendental functions and its referral to Cauchy and Legendre are attested by en.wikipedia; the month is not recorded and October is used only to sit the stop after the residues. Abel's remark is attested by MacTutor to 1826. The reading that Cauchy buried the memoir out of jealousy is later legend, not established fact, and the prose says so.
stops.campa: Niels Henrik Abel, twenty-four and in Paris on a Norwegian grant, leaves at the Academy a memoir on transcendental functions and waits. Cauchy and Legendre are the referees. No report comes. Abel goes home to Norway, poor, and dies of tuberculosis in 1829 without seeing it printed. Of the man holding his manuscript he writes that Cauchy is mad, that nothing can be done about him, and that he is the only one alive who knows how mathematics should be done. The legend that the memoir was buried out of jealousy grows later and is not the same thing as the delay, which is documented.
stops.quote: Cauchy is mad and there is nothing that can be done about him, although, right now, he is the only one who knows how mathematics should be done.
stops.quote_source: Niels Henrik Abel, on visiting the Institute, 1826, quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics
suggested_refs: Abel's Memoire sur une propriete generale d'une classe tres etendue de fonctions transcendantes (1826), printed only in 1841
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Institut de France, Paris: the memoirs of Evariste Galois
stops.date_confidence: attested for the submissions of 25 May and 1 June 1829, for Cauchy and Poinsot as referees, and for the loss of the manuscripts. Rene Taton's 1971 reconstruction of the Academy registers, which suggests Cauchy engaged seriously and that Galois withdrew the papers himself to rework them for the Grand Prix, is cited here at second hand through MacTutor and through evariste_galois.journey.json, and was not opened directly. Coordinates and framing inherited from evariste_galois.journey.json.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of May and again on the first of June, a schoolboy of seventeen named Evariste Galois sends the Academy two memoirs on when an equation can be solved by radicals. Cauchy and Poinsot are named to report. The papers vanish. A century and a half later Rene Taton, reading the Academy's own registers, finds signs that Cauchy took them seriously and that Galois withdrew them himself to rebuild them for the Grand Prix. Neither version can be checked against the manuscripts, because there are no manuscripts. The theory of substitutions the boy is extending is Cauchy's own, begun in the memoir of 1812.
suggested_refs: The proces-verbaux of the Academie des sciences for May and June 1829
Rene Taton's 1971 reconstruction of the Cauchy referral
sources: evariste_galois.journey.json (stop 'Institut de France, the memoirs given to Cauchy and Poinsot', and the Institut pin)
MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Evariste Galois

stops.name: Rue Serpente, Paris: the Lecons and Fourier's series
stops.date_confidence: the 1829 Lecons sur le calcul differentiel, published through De Bure freres and containing one of the first formal definitions of a complex function of a complex variable, is attested by MacTutor and en.wikipedia; the month is not recorded. That Dirichlet's 1829 work on the convergence of Fourier series explicitly corrected errors in an earlier Cauchy attempt is reconstruction, drawn from standard history-of-analysis scholarship as summarized through Belhoste and not re-fetched from a primary paper. The rue Serpente pin is the de Bure family address, itself a reconstruction from Belhoste, used here for the publishing house rather than as a residence scene.
stops.campa: De Bure freres print the Lecons sur le calcul differentiel, in which a function of a complex variable is for the first time formally defined as such: the machinery of the residues is at last given the object it operates on. In the same season his own attempt on the convergence of Joseph Fourier's trigonometric series is corrected in print by Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet. The man who taught Europe to ask whether a series converges had not asked it carefully enough here. Dirichlet supplies the conditions the argument lacked.
suggested_refs: Lecons sur le calcul differentiel (De Bure freres, 1829)
Dirichlet, Sur la convergence des series trigonometriques (1829)
joseph_fourier.journey.json, for the series themselves and the Institute that received them
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Fribourg, Switzerland: the Academie Helvetique that never opens
stops.date_confidence: attested by fr.wikipedia: 'Des les premiers jours de septembre 1830 il s'exile volontairement a Fribourg en Suisse', and by MacTutor and en.wikipedia for the refusal of the oath to Louis-Philippe as the cause. The collapse of the projected Catholic Academie Helvetique is attested by the same French article.
stops.campa: Charles X abdicates in August and the July Monarchy demands an oath of allegiance to Louis-Philippe from everyone it pays. Cauchy does not refuse loudly. He is forty-one. He has resigned nothing formally and has abandoned every post he holds, and will be unemployable in his own country for the next eighteen years. He simply leaves, in the first days of September, without his wife and without his daughters, and goes to Switzerland, to Fribourg, where he joins a scheme for a Catholic Academie Helvetique that never opens its doors.
suggested_refs: The projected Academie Helvetique at Fribourg, 1830-1831
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: University of Turin: the chair the King makes for him
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor and en.wikipedia: the chair of theoretical physics was created for him with the support of the King of Piedmont-Sardinia, teaching began in 1832, and papers went to the Academy of Sciences of Turin from 1831 including material on the integral formula and the residue theorem. The month is not recorded. Menabrea's recollection is attested by MacTutor. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from charles_babbage.journey.json, which pins Turin at 45.0703, 7.6869.
stops.campa: The King of Piedmont-Sardinia makes a chair of theoretical physics for him at Turin, and he begins teaching in 1832, in Italian he is still learning, to a class of thirty. Luigi Federico Menabrea, later prime minister of Italy, is in it, and remembers lectures that jumped without warning from one idea to the next and one formula to another, obscure clouds lit now and then by flashes of pure genius. Of the thirty enrolled, Menabrea writes, he alone saw it through. Meanwhile Cauchy sends the Turin Academy papers carrying the integral formula and the residue theorem in finished form.
stops.quote: were very confused, skipping suddenly from one idea to another, from one formula to the next, with no attempt to give a connection between them. His presentations were obscure clouds, illuminated from time to time by flashes of pure genius. ... of the thirty who enrolled with me, I was the only one to see it through.
stops.quote_source: Luigi Federico Menabrea, recollection of Cauchy's lectures in Turin, quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics

stops.name: Prague: tutor to the Duke of Bordeaux
stops.date_confidence: attested by fr.wikipedia ('Il quitte Turin en juillet 1833 et s'installe a Prague') and by MacTutor and en.wikipedia for the post as scientific tutor to Henri d'Artois, Duke of Bordeaux. The Baron de Damas recruitment letter of 22 June 1833 comes through the dossier and is reconstruction. The barony is attested by en.wikipedia and by fr.wikipedia, which names Charles X as grantor; since Charles X died on 6 November 1836 the grant must predate that, and fr.wikipedia's chaining of it to the 1838 return cannot stand. The 'sewers of Paris' remark is a later comic anecdote in the biographical tradition, not a documented exchange, and the prose labels it as repetition.
stops.campa: A letter from the Baron de Damas reaches him in Turin: the exiled Bourbon court wants a tutor in science for Henri d'Artois, Duke of Bordeaux, grandson of Charles X and, to legitimists, the rightful king of France. He leaves in July and takes the post at Prague. The pupil does not want mathematics. Cauchy mentions once having handled a sewer problem as an engineer, and the boy repeats for years afterward that his tutor began his career in the sewers of Paris. He spends five years drilling a bored adolescent prince in arithmetic, on a salary from a court in exile. The court gives him the title of baron as well.
suggested_refs: The Baron de Damas's letter of recruitment, June 1833
The patent of the barony granted by Charles X before his death in November 1836
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Prague: Bolzano asks to meet
stops.date_confidence: the 1834 meeting at Bolzano's own request is attested through the modern historiographical literature as digested in the dossier; the month is not recorded. The plagiarism controversy over the origin of the definitions of continuity is a disputed later interpretation and is reconstruction, not fact. The publication dates given in the prose, Bolzano 1817 and Cauchy 1821, are themselves attested and are left to speak.
stops.campa: Bernard Bolzano, priest, mathematician, and dismissed professor living quietly in Prague under official suspicion, asks to meet him, and the two men talk. Both have, independently or not, defined continuity in the same terms; Bolzano's Rein analytischer Beweis of 1817 sits beside Cauchy's Cours d'analyse of 1821. Historians will spend the next century arguing whether one took it from the other, and the arithmetic of those two dates makes the charge against Cauchy hard to sustain. What the two of them actually said in the room is not recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: Bolzano, Rein analytischer Beweis (1817)
The modern historiographical literature on the Cauchy-Bolzano question

stops.name: Prague: the family crosses Europe
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1834 by fr.wikipedia ('rejoint par sa femme et ses deux filles en 1834') and by en.wikipedia. The month is not recorded. Nothing about the journey itself, or about what passed by letter in the preceding four years, survives in any source reached.
stops.campa: Aloise de Bure crosses Europe with Marie-Francoise Alicia and Marie-Mathilde and joins him in Prague. It is nearly four years since he walked out of Paris alone. The daughters are fifteen and eleven. The household is together again in a foreign city, on a salary paid by a king with no country. What was said between them by letter across the Alps and the Bohemian frontier has not survived in any quantity, and what was said when they arrived is not recorded at all.
suggested_refs: The Cauchy family correspondence of 1830-1834, largely unpublished

stops.name: Teplice, Bohemia: the court on the move
stops.date_confidence: attested by fr.wikipedia, which lists Toeplitz among the exiled court's stops for 1835. The month is not recorded and June is used only to order the itinerary. That his output slowed in these years is the standard biographical account rather than a counted fact.
stops.campa: The court does not stay put. It moves to Teplice in northern Bohemia, a spa town of hot springs and visiting German princes, and the tutor moves with it. He is forty-six. He keeps his seat at the Academie des sciences in Paris the whole time; it is the one appointment in France that never required an oath from anybody. His output slows almost to nothing in these years: no library, no Academy, no colleague to argue with, and a pupil to be taught every day.
suggested_refs: The itinerary of the exiled Bourbon court in Bohemia, 1833-1838

stops.name: Gorlitz, Silesia: the itinerant tutor
stops.date_confidence: attested by fr.wikipedia, which gives 'en 1836 a Budweitz, Kirchberg et Gorlitz' among the court's stops; Gorlitz was then in Prussian Silesia. The month is not recorded. Coordinate corrected from the research pool's 51.1642, 14.9857 to the OSM value for the town centre, about 960 m to the south-east. Kirchberg, also a 1836 stop, is omitted here for want of a coordinate and is named in the report.
stops.campa: The itinerary carries the household on again, to Budweis, to Kirchberg, and then to Gorlitz on the Neisse in Prussian Silesia. Six years out of France. He is a baron of a court that governs nothing, drawing a foreign salary in a Prussian border town and tutoring a claimant nobody will crown. The Duke of Bordeaux turns sixteen this year, and the tutorship ends when he turns eighteen. In Paris his chairs are filled by other men and his name is on nothing new.
suggested_refs: Gorlitz on the Neisse, Prussian Silesia, a stop of the exiled court in 1836

stops.name: Paris: the return from eight years
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia for the end of the tutorship in September 1838 when the Duke turned eighteen, and by MacTutor and en.wikipedia for the return to Paris, the recovery of the Academie seat, and the exclusion from teaching and salaried university roles for refusing the oath. The month of the return is not recorded and October orders the segment. The Comptes rendus page limit is a standard biographical detail, not re-verified in this pass. Coordinates inherited from alexis_de_tocqueville.journey.json, which pins Paris at 48.8566, 2.3522.
stops.campa: The Duke turns eighteen in September and the tutorship ends with him. Cauchy comes home to Paris after eight years. His seat at the Academie des sciences is still his; every other post in France is shut, because every other post requires the oath to Louis-Philippe and he will not swear it. He is forty-nine and legally barred from teaching anywhere in France. What he does instead is publish. Papers go into the Academy's Comptes rendus week after week, at a rate that eventually forces the journal to impose a page limit.
suggested_refs: The Comptes rendus hebdomadaires de l'Academie des sciences, 1838 onward
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Observatoire de Paris: elected to the Bureau des Longitudes, and not seated
stops.date_confidence: attested for November 1839 by en.wikipedia and MacTutor: elected, then denied the appointment and salary for refusing the oath, and replaced by Louis Poinsot at the end of 1843. The names of the backers, Biot and Arago, and of the opponent, Poisson, come through the dossier's citation of a modern Bureau des Longitudes historical project that treats the episode as an election not validated; that project page was not opened directly in this pass.
stops.campa: He stands for the Bureau des Longitudes and wins. Biot backs him; so does Arago, who agrees with him about nothing political. Poisson opposes. The election is carried and then not validated: the government will not confirm a man who has not sworn, so he is elected to a body he cannot sit in and paid nothing for a seat that is legally his. Nobody has to order the punishment; the rule runs by itself on whoever will not say the words. He attends anyway, and works, for four years. At the end of 1843 Louis Poinsot is put in his place.
suggested_refs: The Bureau des Longitudes registers for the 1839 election and its non-validation
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Institut de France, Paris: the Exercices d'analyse
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor for the four-volume Exercices d'analyse et de physique mathematique beginning in 1840 and appearing across the decade, and for the figure of 789 papers in the collected works. The month is not recorded. fr.wikipedia rounds the paper count to 'pres de 800 parutions'; the discrepancy is flagged in the report and the MacTutor figure is used.
stops.campa: With no chair and no salary, he opens a new serial: the Exercices d'analyse et de physique mathematique, four volumes across the decade, written by himself and paid for by himself. Elasticity, light, the mechanics of continua, the convergence of everything. He is producing at a rate no institution asked for and none can stop. The Academy is his only remaining employer and it pays him nothing. By the count in the collected works he will leave seven hundred and eighty-nine papers behind him.
suggested_refs: Exercices d'analyse et de physique mathematique, 4 vols. (1840-1847)
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Augustin-Louis Cauchy

stops.name: Paris: La Chandeleur
stops.date_confidence: attested: the piece 'La Chandeleur' appeared in the Bulletin de l'Institut Catholique on 1 February 1843 and is quoted in Belhoste (1991), ch. 13, as reproduced on Wikiquote. The place of writing is not recorded; the generic Paris pin is used.
stops.campa: He writes for the Bulletin de l'Institut Catholique a piece for Candlemas, and lets out something the memoirs never show. The piece appears on the first of February. He is fifty-three, in the middle of the most prolific decade of his life, publishing weekly, unpaid, unemployed by the state. There is no let up, he writes, no end to it, accursed problems, innumerable calculations, endless fighting, signs, formulas, theorems besetting him from dawn to dusk.
stops.quote: There is no let up! No end to it! Accursed problems! Innumerable calculations. Endless fighting. Signs. Formulas. Theorems besetting me from dawn to dusk!
stops.quote_source: Augustin-Louis Cauchy, 'La Chandeleur', Bulletin de l'Institut Catholique, 1 February 1843, quoted in Belhoste (1991), ch. 13, as reproduced on Wikiquote

stops.name: College de France, Paris: the chair goes to Libri
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1843 by MacTutor and by en.wikipedia's article on Guglielmo Libri for the College de France succession after Lacroix's death, with Cauchy, Liouville and Libri as the candidates and Libri chosen; the month is not recorded and May is used to order the segment. Liouville's letter of the following day is attested by MacTutor. Libri's later exposure as a thief of library manuscripts is attested by en.wikipedia.
stops.campa: Lacroix dies and his mathematics chair at the College de France is open. Cauchy stands. So do Joseph Liouville and Guglielmo Libri. Cauchy's Jesuit sympathies and his open Catholic campaigning are held against him, and the chair goes to Libri, who will be exposed five years later as a thief of manuscripts and rare books from the public libraries of France and will flee to England with the loot. Liouville, who lost too, writes the next day that he is deeply humiliated as a man and as a mathematician by what took place.
stops.quote: deeply humiliated as a man and as a mathematician by what took place yesterday at the College de France.
stops.quote_source: Joseph Liouville, letter written the day after Libri's 1843 appointment over Cauchy to the College de France chair, quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics

stops.name: Faculte des sciences de Paris: reinstated
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia gives the formal reinstatement as professor of mathematical astronomy at the Faculte des sciences de Paris on 1 March 1849, once the oath requirement had been abolished after the 1848 revolution; MacTutor corroborates the 1848-1849 return. Coordinate corrected from the research pool's 48.8467, 2.3431 to the OSM value for the Centre Sorbonne at 17 rue de la Sorbonne; the pool's value fell about 210 m south, near rue Cujas.
stops.campa: Louis-Philippe falls in February 1848 and the Second Republic abolishes the oath. The bar that kept him out of every paid post in France for eighteen years is simply gone, removed by a revolution he did not want and did not make. On the first of March 1849 he is installed as professor of mathematical astronomy in the Faculte des sciences de Paris. It is the first salary the French state has paid him since 1830, and he will hold the chair until he dies. He is fifty-nine.

stops.name: College de France, Paris: the chair lost to Liouville
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1850 by MacTutor for the loss of a chair election to Joseph Liouville; the month is not recorded. The characterization of the running Cauchy-Liouville quarrel over priority and Academy business is the standard biographical account rather than a single sourced claim.
stops.campa: He stands once more for a chair at the College de France and loses it to Joseph Liouville. Libri, who beat them both in 1843, has by now fled to England ahead of a conviction for stealing manuscripts from the public libraries of France, so the chair the two of them are contesting is one a thief took from them first. Against Liouville, Cauchy will keep a running quarrel for the rest of the decade, over priority and over the conduct of the Academy's business.

stops.name: Paris: Considerations sur les ordres religieux
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1850 for the pamphlet, published by Pommeret et Moreau; the quotation is from p. 26, in the translation by Julio Antonio Gonzalo in The Intelligible Universe (World Scientific, 2008), p. 301, as given on Wikiquote. The month is not recorded. A companion sentence on the same page, naming Corneille, Racine, Bossuet and Fenelon, is quoted on Wikiquote in a rendering with visible OCR damage and is not used.
stops.campa: He publishes the Considerations sur les ordres religieux adressees aux amis des sciences, a defence of the teaching orders written by a member of the Academie des sciences at the moment when the Republic is deciding who may be allowed to run a school. In it he puts himself in a line: Brahe, Copernicus, Descartes, Newton, Fermat, Leibniz, Pascal, Euler. He is not arguing that religion and science are compatible. He is naming the men who did both, and asking what exactly is supposed to be new about him.
stops.quote: I am a Christian, that is, I believe in the divinity of Christ, as did Tycho Brahe, Copernicus, Descartes, Newton, Fermat, Leibniz, Pascal, Grimaldi, Euler, Guldin, Boscovich, Gerdil, as did all the great astronomers, physicist and geometricians of past ages.
stops.quote_source: Augustin-Louis Cauchy, Considerations sur les ordres religieux adressees aux amis des sciences (Pommeret et Moreau, 1850), p. 26, translated by Julio Antonio Gonzalo in The Intelligible Universe (World Scientific, 2008), p. 301, quoted on Wikiquote

stops.name: Paris: the minister and the Emperor
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1852 by en.wikipedia, whose wording is: 'This time a cabinet minister was able to convince the Emperor to exempt Cauchy from the oath.' The research pool's chronology overstated this as a personal decree of Napoleon III on his own initiative; the corrected version is used. The month is not recorded. The American Academy of Arts and Sciences election (1832) and the American Philosophical Society election (1853) are both attested by en.wikipedia.
stops.campa: Louis-Napoleon takes the empire and a new oath comes with it. Cauchy will not swear this one either, and at sixty-three he is prepared to lose the chair he waited eighteen years for. A cabinet minister goes to the Emperor and gets him exempted personally. The regime that had every reason to break him decides instead to write him out of its own rule, and he keeps the Sorbonne. Foreign bodies go on electing him regardless of who governs Paris: the American Academy of Arts and Sciences took him during the Turin exile, the American Philosophical Society takes him in 1853.
suggested_refs: The imperial exemption of 1852 from the Second Empire loyalty oath

stops.name: Paris: the Oeuvre des Ecoles d'Orient
stops.date_confidence: attested to 4 April 1856 through the modern Oeuvre d'Orient's own historical presentation and a Bibliotheque nationale de France listing of founding professors that names Cauchy among them, both reached via the working dossier rather than opened directly in this pass. The founders named, Lenormant, Falloux, Montalembert and Ravignan, come from the same source. The pin is a generic central Paris address; the founding venue is not recorded in the material reached.
stops.campa: On the fourth of April, with Charles Lenormant, Alfred de Falloux, Montalembert and the preacher Xavier de Ravignan, he founds an organisation to fund French Christian schools in the Ottoman East. The Crimean War has just ended and the question of who protects the Christians of the Levant is live in Paris. He is sixty-six, holds a chair at last, and gives his working evenings to the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul, to famine relief for Ireland, and now to this. The body outlives him and still operates, under the name Oeuvre d'Orient.

stops.name: Sceaux: the girls' school and the patronage
stops.date_confidence: attested by sceaux-lagazette.fr, which reports that Cauchy financed a girls' school and a boys' patronage at Sceaux in his final years and gives the mayor Edmond Guyon's funeral tribute to his care for 'the elderly, children, all that is interesting and weak'. The date is given only as the 1850s; January 1855 orders the segment and should not be quoted. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from eugene_grasset.journey.json and the other Sceaux files.
stops.campa: In the town he has summered in for more than thirty years he pays for a school for girls and a patronage for boys, out of a professor's salary and whatever the books bring in. None of this appears in a paper or a memoir; it is a household in a suburb spending its money on the town it lives in, and almost nobody writing about him has bothered with it. The mayor, Edmond Guyon, will say over his grave that he cared for the elderly, for children, for all that is interesting and weak.

stops.name: Sceaux, the house in the grounds of the Lycee Marie-Curie: the last morning
stops.date_confidence: the date and place are attested: fr.wikipedia gives 'Le 23 mai, vers 4 h du matin, il meurt d'un rhume dans la maison familiale de sa femme a Sceaux', and sceaux-lagazette.fr identifies the house as one still standing within the grounds of the Lycee Marie-Curie. Source pairing is loose: sceaux-lagazette gives neither the four o'clock hour nor the cause, both of which come from en.wikipedia and MacTutor. The deathbed account is his daughter's letter, printed in Valson (1868) and reproduced by MacTutor: later family testimony, not an independent record. Coordinate corrected from the research pool's 48.7784, 2.2903 to the OSM value for the Lycee Marie Curie at 1 rue Constant Pilate, about 220 m away.
stops.campa: His physician sends him out of Paris in the spring for the air. He goes to Sceaux, to the family house, with a bronchial complaint he does not recover from. His daughter's account has him fully lucid until half past three in the morning, when he says the names of Jesus, Mary and Joseph and appears for the first time to understand what is happening to him. At about four o'clock he dies. He is sixty-seven. He had been at the Academy in Paris weeks before, quarrelling with Duhamel over who first solved the problem of inelastic shocks.
stops.quote: Having remained fully alert, in complete control of his mental powers, until 3.30 a.m., my father suddenly uttered the blessed names of Jesus, Mary and Joseph. For the first time, he seemed to be aware of the gravity of his condition. At about four o'clock, his soul went to God. He met his death with such calm that made us ashamed of our unhappiness.
stops.quote_source: Letter by Cauchy's daughter describing his death, quoted in C.-A. Valson, La vie et les travaux du baron Cauchy (Paris, 1868), as reproduced in MacTutor History of Mathematics

stops.name: Cimetiere de Sceaux: the burial
stops.date_confidence: the burial at the cimetiere de Sceaux is attested by fr.wikipedia and sceaux-lagazette.fr; the exact day is not recorded and 26 May orders the sequence. The exact plot within the cemetery is unknown to every source reached and is stated as a gap. sceaux-lagazette.fr confirms the mayor's tribute and that the funeral drew prominent scientists from Paris, but does not name the Institut, the Sorbonne and the College de France specifically, so the prose does not either. The Oeuvres completes run to 27 volumes 1882-1974 by en.wikipedia, 28 volumes over the same span by fr.wikipedia, and 27 volumes 1882-1970 by MacTutor; the campa carries the disagreement rather than resolving it.
stops.campa: He is buried in the cemetery of Sceaux and not in Paris. Scholars come out from Paris for the funeral and the mayor speaks. His name will be one of the seventy-two cut into the Eiffel Tower, on a monument raised thirty-two years after his death, in a France whose oaths he had twice declined to swear. What he left takes another hundred and seventeen years to print: the Oeuvres completes begin appearing under the Academy in 1882 and are not finished until 1974, twenty-seven volumes by one count and twenty-eight by another. The exact plot is not recorded in anything that survives.
